title: Roseate Spoonbill
summary: A spectacular pink wading bird of shallow South Florida wetlands.
identification: Large pink body, long legs, and a flat spoon-shaped bill. Adults show brighter pink wings and shoulders.
habitat: Mangroves, tidal flats, marshes, lagoons, and shallow ponds.
diet: Small fish, shrimp, aquatic insects, and other tiny wetland animals.
photography: Photograph at eye level near shallow feeding water. Early light helps preserve detail in the bright pink feathers.
fact: Its pink color comes largely from pigments obtained through its diet.

title: Great Blue Heron
summary: Florida’s largest commonly seen heron and a patient wetland hunter.
identification: Very large gray-blue heron with a long neck, heavy bill, and dark head stripe.
habitat: Freshwater and coastal wetlands, canals, ponds, mangroves, and shorelines.
diet: Fish, frogs, snakes, insects, and small mammals.
photography: Watch for the slow stalking pose, then use a fast shutter speed when the bird strikes.
fact: Despite its size, it can perch and nest high in trees.

title: Great Egret
summary: A tall white egret found throughout Florida wetlands.
identification: Long black legs, yellow bill, and all-white plumage; breeding adults grow long back plumes.
habitat: Marshes, ponds, canals, estuaries, and mangrove edges.
diet: Fish, frogs, crustaceans, insects, and small reptiles.
photography: Meter carefully for white feathers and avoid overexposure in direct sun.
fact: Its elegant breeding plumes once made it a target of the feather trade.

title: Snowy Egret
summary: A lively small egret known for its bright yellow feet.
identification: White plumage, black bill and legs, and yellow feet that look like golden slippers.
habitat: Shallow freshwater and coastal wetlands.
diet: Small fish, shrimp, insects, and other aquatic prey.
photography: Use continuous autofocus because Snowy Egrets often run, hop, and stir the water while feeding.
fact: It may shake or shuffle its feet to flush hidden prey.

title: Little Blue Heron
summary: A slender heron whose juveniles begin life completely white.
identification: Adults are slate-blue with a purplish neck; young birds are white and gradually become mottled.
habitat: Marshes, ponds, canals, flooded fields, and mangroves.
diet: Fish, frogs, crustaceans, and insects.
photography: Look for clean reflections in calm water and wait for the bird to extend its neck.
fact: The white juvenile plumage may help young birds feed near other white herons.

title: Tricolored Heron
summary: An active, slender heron common in South Florida wetlands.
identification: Blue-gray upperparts, white belly, rusty neck tones, and a long pointed bill.
habitat: Coastal marshes, mangroves, estuaries, ponds, and shallow wetlands.
diet: Small fish, crustaceans, and aquatic insects.
photography: A fast shutter speed is useful because it often darts and changes direction while hunting.
fact: Its white belly is a useful field mark when separated from other dark herons.

title: Green Heron
summary: A compact and secretive heron often found along vegetated shorelines.
identification: Stocky body, dark greenish back, chestnut neck, and relatively short legs.
habitat: Ponds, canals, mangroves, wooded swamps, and quiet wetland edges.
diet: Fish, frogs, insects, and crustaceans.
photography: Scan low branches and shaded banks; a longer lens helps avoid disturbing this cautious bird.
fact: Green Herons sometimes drop small objects on the water as bait.

title: White Ibis
summary: One of South Florida’s most familiar wading birds.
identification: Adults are white with black wing tips, a curved reddish bill, and pink-red legs.
habitat: Lawns, marshes, mangroves, mudflats, and shallow ponds.
diet: Crayfish, insects, small fish, crabs, and other invertebrates.
photography: Photograph small groups feeding together and expose carefully for white plumage.
fact: Young White Ibises are brown and gradually become white as they mature.

title: Wood Stork
summary: A large wetland bird with broad black-and-white wings.
identification: White body, black flight feathers, long legs, and a bare dark head in adults.
habitat: Shallow freshwater wetlands, marshes, swamps, and retention ponds.
diet: Fish and other aquatic animals detected by touch.
photography: Flight photographs work well when the bird circles on rising warm air.
fact: It catches prey by snapping its bill shut when something touches the inside.

title: Anhinga
summary: A diving bird often seen drying its wings beside Florida water.
identification: Long snake-like neck, pointed bill, dark body, and silvery wing pattern in males.
habitat: Freshwater ponds, canals, lakes, marshes, and slow rivers.
diet: Fish and other aquatic animals.
photography: Wait for wing-drying poses or photograph the head and neck emerging from the water.
fact: Its low-floating body can make the neck look like a snake moving across the surface.

title: Double-crested Cormorant
summary: A dark waterbird frequently seen swimming, diving, and resting on posts.
identification: Dark body, hooked bill, orange facial skin, and a thicker neck than an Anhinga.
habitat: Lakes, canals, coastal waters, ponds, and reservoirs.
diet: Mostly fish.
photography: Use a fast shutter for takeoff sequences because the bird often runs across the water.
fact: The small feather crests that give it its name are easiest to see during breeding season.

title: Osprey
summary: A fish-eating raptor common near water throughout Florida.
identification: White underparts, dark brown back, bold dark eye stripe, and long angled wings.
habitat: Coasts, lakes, rivers, canals, and wetlands with nearby nesting structures.
diet: Almost entirely fish.
photography: Track the bird before a dive and use high-speed burst mode for splash and lift-off sequences.
fact: Its reversible outer toe helps it hold slippery fish.

title: Red-shouldered Hawk
summary: A vocal woodland hawk commonly seen in Florida neighborhoods and wetlands.
identification: Reddish barred chest, black-and-white wing pattern, and a banded tail.
habitat: Wooded wetlands, suburban tree cover, hammocks, and forest edges.
diet: Small mammals, frogs, snakes, lizards, and insects.
photography: Listen for repeated calls and check exposed branches near wet areas.
fact: Florida birds often appear paler than many Red-shouldered Hawks farther north.

title: Belted Kingfisher
summary: A fast-flying fishing bird with a loud rattling call.
identification: Large head, shaggy crest, blue-gray upperparts, and a white collar; females also have a rusty belly band.
habitat: Canals, ponds, rivers, estuaries, and coastlines.
diet: Fish and aquatic animals.
photography: Pre-focus near a favorite perch and use a high shutter speed for diving action.
fact: Females are more colorful than males, unusual among many bird species.

title: Northern Cardinal
summary: A familiar songbird and year-round resident across Florida.
identification: Males are bright red; females are warm brown with red highlights. Both have a crest and thick orange bill.
habitat: Gardens, shrubs, woodland edges, parks, and neighborhoods.
diet: Seeds, fruits, and insects.
photography: Use shrubs as a natural frame and wait for soft morning or late-afternoon light.
fact: Both males and females sing.

title: Blue Jay
summary: A bold and intelligent backyard bird with striking blue markings.
identification: Blue upperparts, white face and underside, black necklace, and prominent crest.
habitat: Woodlands, parks, neighborhoods, and oak-rich habitats.
diet: Seeds, nuts, insects, fruits, and varied foods.
photography: Expose for the white face and photograph against uncluttered foliage when possible.
fact: The blue color is structural, created by the way feathers scatter light rather than by blue pigment.

title: Red-bellied Woodpecker
summary: A common Florida woodpecker with a barred black-and-white back.
identification: Red crown or nape, pale face, zebra-patterned back, and a faint reddish wash on the belly.
habitat: Woodlands, palms, parks, gardens, and suburban areas.
diet: Insects, fruits, nuts, seeds, and sap.
photography: Watch trunks and palm trees; use continuous autofocus as it moves around the far side of a trunk.
fact: Its name refers to the subtle red belly patch, not the much more obvious red head markings.

title: Northern Mockingbird
summary: Florida’s state bird and a talented mimic.
identification: Gray body, pale underside, long tail, and bold white wing patches visible in flight.
habitat: Neighborhoods, parks, open woodland, fields, and scrub.
diet: Insects, fruits, and berries.
photography: Look for singing birds on exposed posts and branches, especially in spring.
fact: One bird may imitate many other species and repeat each phrase several times.

title: Mourning Dove
summary: A graceful dove whose soft call is common across Florida.
identification: Slim buff-gray body, small head, black wing spots, and long pointed tail.
habitat: Open woodland, yards, fields, roadsides, and urban areas.
diet: Mostly seeds.
photography: Use gentle light and a quiet approach; the delicate eye ring and feather patterns show best at close range.
fact: Its wings make a distinctive whistling sound during takeoff.

title: Painted Bunting
summary: A small winter visitor whose male is among North America’s most colorful birds.
identification: Males show blue, green, and red; females are bright yellow-green.
habitat: Thickets, brushy edges, coastal hammocks, and feeders during the cooler months.
diet: Seeds and insects.
photography: Photograph in open shade to preserve saturated color and avoid harsh highlights.
fact: Females and young birds can be difficult to spot because their green plumage blends into foliage.

title: Zebra Longwing
summary: Florida’s state butterfly, recognized by long black wings with yellow stripes.
identification: Long narrow black wings crossed by pale yellow bands; slow, graceful flight.
habitat: Shaded gardens, hammocks, forest edges, and areas with passionvine.
diet: Adults take nectar and also collect pollen; caterpillars feed on passionvines.
photography: Use a moderate shutter speed while it hovers at flowers, or photograph roosting groups early in the morning.
fact: Unlike most butterflies, adults can digest pollen, helping them live for several months.

title: Monarch
summary: A famous orange-and-black butterfly found in Florida gardens and natural areas.
identification: Orange wings with black veins and a black border dotted with white.
habitat: Gardens, open fields, roadsides, and places with milkweed and nectar plants.
diet: Adults drink nectar; caterpillars eat milkweed.
photography: Include native milkweed or flowering plants to tell a stronger habitat story.
fact: Florida supports both resident Monarchs and seasonal migrants.

title: Gulf Fritillary
summary: A brilliant orange butterfly common around passionvine.
identification: Orange upperwings with black spots; silver-white spots cover the brown underside.
habitat: Gardens, fields, roadsides, and disturbed areas with passionvine.
diet: Adults take nectar; caterpillars eat passionvine leaves.
photography: Try backlighting to reveal the glowing orange wings and silver underside spots.
fact: Its caterpillar is orange with dark spines but is harmless to touch.

title: Julia Butterfly
summary: A long-winged orange butterfly of tropical South Florida.
identification: Narrow bright orange wings; males are usually more vivid than females.
habitat: Gardens, hammocks, forest edges, and areas with passionvine.
diet: Nectar; caterpillars feed on passionvines.
photography: Use continuous autofocus because Julias often glide rapidly between flowers.
fact: It is closely associated with warm climates and is especially common in southern Florida.

title: White Peacock
summary: A pale butterfly frequently seen low over South Florida wetlands and gardens.
identification: White wings with brown markings and small orange and blue eyespots.
habitat: Wetland edges, gardens, canals, roadsides, and open disturbed habitats.
diet: Nectar; caterpillars feed on several low-growing wetland plants.
photography: Photograph from a low angle because it often lands near the ground.
fact: Adults are territorial and may repeatedly return to the same sunny patch.

title: Common Buckeye
summary: A ground-loving butterfly marked with prominent eyespots.
identification: Brown wings with large colorful eyespots and orange bars.
habitat: Open fields, roadsides, gardens, and sunny disturbed areas.
diet: Nectar; caterpillars use plantain, snapdragon relatives, and other host plants.
photography: Approach slowly while it basks with wings open in sunny areas.
fact: The dramatic eyespots may help startle or distract predators.

title: Giant Swallowtail
summary: North America’s largest butterfly and a regular visitor to Florida citrus.
identification: Large dark wings crossed by yellow bands; underside is mostly yellow.
habitat: Gardens, citrus groves, hammocks, and woodland edges.
diet: Adults drink nectar; caterpillars eat citrus-family plants.
photography: Use a fast shutter because it often feeds while continuously beating its wings.
fact: The caterpillar resembles bird droppings, an effective camouflage strategy.

title: Eastern Black Swallowtail
summary: A dark swallowtail often associated with parsley-family plants.
identification: Black wings with rows of pale yellow spots; females have more blue on the hindwings.
habitat: Gardens, fields, roadsides, and open habitats.
diet: Nectar; caterpillars eat parsley, dill, fennel, and native relatives.
photography: Photograph freshly emerged adults early in the day when they are less active.
fact: The caterpillar has an orange forked scent organ called an osmeterium.

title: Cloudless Sulphur
summary: A large yellow butterfly that moves quickly through Florida landscapes.
identification: Bright lemon-yellow male; females vary from pale yellow to whitish with dark markings.
habitat: Gardens, open areas, roadsides, and places with cassia or senna host plants.
diet: Nectar; caterpillars eat senna and cassia plants.
photography: Use high-speed burst mode as it rarely stays still for long.
fact: Large seasonal movements can bring many Cloudless Sulphurs through South Florida.

title: Queen Butterfly
summary: A rich brown-orange relative of the Monarch.
identification: Chestnut wings with black borders and white spots; forewings have dark veins.
habitat: Open fields, gardens, coastal areas, and habitats with milkweed-family plants.
diet: Nectar; caterpillars feed on milkweed relatives.
photography: Side lighting brings out the velvety brown-orange color and white spotting.
fact: Its chemical defenses come from compounds obtained from larval host plants.

title: Eastern Pondhawk
summary: A common and assertive dragonfly around Florida ponds.
identification: Mature males are powder blue; females and young males are bright green with dark abdominal marks.
habitat: Ponds, lakes, canals, and marsh edges.
diet: Flying insects, including other dragonflies.
photography: Watch for repeated returns to the same perch and pre-focus on that spot.
fact: It is a powerful predator capable of catching insects nearly its own size.

title: Blue Dasher
summary: A small blue dragonfly often perched with wings angled forward.
identification: Males develop a blue abdomen and dark thorax; females are patterned yellow and black.
habitat: Still ponds, marshes, canals, and garden water features.
diet: Small flying insects.
photography: A close-focusing telephoto or macro lens works well from a respectful distance.
fact: Males often choose a favorite exposed perch and defend it.

title: Halloween Pennant
summary: A striking orange-winged dragonfly found around grassy wetlands.
identification: Orange wings with dark brown bands and a slender orange body.
habitat: Ponds, marshes, lakes, and wet meadows.
diet: Small flying insects.
photography: Photograph on grass tips when breezes pause; keep the background distant and soft.
fact: Its festive orange-and-brown pattern inspired its common name.

title: Great Blue Skimmer
summary: A large dragonfly of shaded ponds and wooded wetlands.
identification: Mature males are pale blue; females and young males are brown with a dark stripe along the abdomen.
habitat: Wooded ponds, swamps, slow streams, and shady wetland edges.
diet: Flying insects.
photography: Look along shaded perches and use a higher ISO rather than sacrificing shutter speed.
fact: It is one of the larger blue skimmers commonly encountered in Florida.

title: Common Green Darner
summary: A large, strong-flying green dragonfly and long-distance migrant.
identification: Green thorax, large body, and clear wings; males usually have a blue abdomen.
habitat: Ponds, marshes, lakes, and open areas during migration.
diet: Flying insects.
photography: Flight shots require fast autofocus, high shutter speed, and practice tracking erratic movement.
fact: Some populations migrate over great distances across North America.

title: Widow Skimmer
summary: A bold skimmer with dark patches at the base of each wing.
identification: Males develop a powder-blue abdomen and white wing bands beyond the dark basal patches.
habitat: Ponds, lakes, ditches, and open wetlands.
diet: Small flying insects.
photography: Side views show the dramatic wing pattern best; wait for a clean perch.
fact: The dark-and-white wing markings make mature males especially distinctive.

title: American Alligator
summary: Florida’s iconic freshwater reptile and an important wetland engineer.
identification: Broad rounded snout, dark body, and only upper teeth usually visible when the mouth is closed.
habitat: Marshes, ponds, canals, lakes, swamps, and slow rivers.
diet: Fish, turtles, birds, mammals, and other available prey.
photography: Use a long lens, remain well back from the shoreline, and never feed or approach an alligator.
fact: Alligator holes can retain water during dry periods and provide refuge for many other animals.

title: American Crocodile
summary: A rare native crocodilian found mainly in far South Florida.
identification: Narrower pointed snout, gray-green coloration, and both upper and lower teeth may show when the mouth is closed.
habitat: Brackish and saltwater habitats, mangrove creeks, bays, and coastal lagoons.
diet: Fish, crustaceans, birds, and other animals.
photography: Observe only from a safe distance with a long lens and follow all posted wildlife rules.
fact: South Florida is the only place in the United States where alligators and crocodiles naturally coexist.

title: Florida Softshell Turtle
summary: A large aquatic turtle with a flattened leathery shell and snorkel-like nose.
identification: Flat oval shell, long neck, pointed tubular snout, and webbed feet.
habitat: Ponds, canals, lakes, marshes, and slow-moving water.
diet: Fish, insects, crustaceans, snails, and other aquatic prey.
photography: Photograph basking turtles from a distance before they slide back into the water.
fact: It can remain mostly buried in mud or sand with only its nose exposed.

title: North American River Otter
summary: A playful but elusive mammal of Florida’s waterways.
identification: Sleek dark brown body, long muscular tail, short legs, and whiskered face.
habitat: Rivers, marshes, canals, lakes, mangroves, and wetlands.
diet: Fish, crayfish, frogs, and other aquatic animals.
photography: Be ready with fast settings; otters appear briefly and move quickly between dives.
fact: Family groups may travel and play together, sometimes using the same shoreline routes repeatedly.

title: Marsh Rabbit
summary: A small dark rabbit adapted to Florida wetlands.
identification: Compact brown body, relatively small ears, and a dark underside to the tail.
habitat: Marshes, wet prairies, mangrove edges, and dense vegetation near water.
diet: Grasses, sedges, aquatic plants, and other vegetation.
photography: Search quietly near vegetation at dawn or dusk and keep movement slow.
fact: It is a capable swimmer and may enter water to escape danger.

title: Firebush
summary: A native shrub whose tubular flowers attract hummingbirds and butterflies.
identification: Clusters of orange-red tubular flowers, reddish stems, and opposite or whorled leaves.
habitat: Hammocks, pinelands, coastal areas, and Florida-friendly gardens.
diet: This plant is a nectar source rather than an animal diet subject.
photography: Use a macro or telephoto lens to include visiting pollinators and isolate flower clusters.
fact: Its long blooming season makes it especially valuable in wildlife gardens.

title: Pickerelweed
summary: A native aquatic plant with spikes of violet-blue flowers.
identification: Heart-shaped leaves and upright flower spikes covered with small purple-blue blooms.
habitat: Shallow freshwater wetlands, pond edges, marshes, and canals.
diet: Provides nectar, cover, and seeds used by wetland wildlife.
photography: Photograph low across the water to combine flowers, reflections, and visiting insects.
fact: Its dense growth provides habitat for many small aquatic animals.

title: Bald Cypress
summary: A long-lived wetland tree famous for flared trunks and cypress knees.
identification: Tall deciduous conifer with feathery leaves, buttressed base, and woody knees in wet soil.
habitat: Swamps, floodplains, pond margins, and slow waterways.
diet: Not applicable; it supports wildlife through habitat, seeds, and shelter.
photography: Fog, reflections, and backlight can create strong landscape photographs in cypress wetlands.
fact: Although it is a conifer, it sheds its leaves each year.

title: Gumbo Limbo
summary: A distinctive tropical tree often called the tourist tree.
identification: Smooth copper-red peeling bark and compound green leaves.
habitat: Coastal hammocks and tropical landscapes in South Florida.
diet: Its fruits are eaten by birds and other wildlife.
photography: Side lighting emphasizes the colorful peeling bark and sculptural trunk.
fact: The nickname tourist tree refers to its red, peeling “sunburned” bark.

title: Sabal Palm
summary: Florida’s state tree and a defining feature of the state’s landscapes.
identification: Tall palm with fan-shaped leaves and a trunk that may retain old leaf bases.
habitat: Hammocks, flatwoods, coastal areas, wetlands, and developed landscapes.
diet: Flowers and fruit provide resources for insects, birds, and mammals.
photography: Use wide compositions at sunrise or sunset, or frame wildlife among the fronds.
fact: Despite being called a tree, palms are structurally different from woody broadleaf trees.

title: Photographing Florida Birds
summary: Practical field techniques for sharper, more natural bird photographs.
identification: Use bird behavior, posture, and habitat as identification clues before approaching.
habitat: Wetlands, beaches, gardens, and wooded edges each require different working distances and backgrounds.
diet: Not applicable.
photography: Favor early or late light, continuous autofocus, eye detection, and shutter speeds appropriate to the bird’s movement. Keep a respectful distance and never block an animal’s escape route.
fact: Learning repeated behaviors often produces better photographs than simply following a moving bird.

title: Butterfly Photography in Florida
summary: A field guide to photographing butterflies without disturbing them.
identification: Notice wing shape, pattern, and host plants to help identify the subject.
habitat: Gardens, roadsides, hammocks, wetlands, and native plant areas.
diet: Not applicable.
photography: Work during cooler mornings when butterflies are less active. Keep the camera parallel to the wings when maximum detail is desired and avoid casting a shadow over the insect.
fact: A slightly longer macro lens can provide good magnification while preserving working distance.

title: Everglades Photography Guide
summary: Planning, safety, and composition ideas for photographing the Everglades.
identification: Learn the difference between common wading birds, alligators, crocodiles, and wetland habitats.
habitat: Sawgrass marsh, sloughs, hardwood hammocks, mangroves, cypress domes, and coastal estuaries.
diet: Not applicable.
photography: Carry water, sun protection, and rain protection. Use long lenses for wildlife, wide lenses for habitat, and watch changing skies without approaching dangerous animals.
fact: The Everglades is a slow-moving river of grass rather than a simple stagnant swamp.

title: Canon EOS R6 Mark II Wildlife Settings
summary: A flexible starting point for birds, mammals, and fast action with the Canon R6 Mark II.
identification: Identification depends on the subject; use eye detection as an aid, not a replacement for field knowledge.
habitat: Adapt settings to light, background, subject distance, and movement.
diet: Not applicable.
photography: Try Servo AF with subject detection, high-speed continuous shooting, Auto ISO, and a shutter speed around 1/1600 second for active birds. Reduce speed for still subjects and raise it for flight or splashing action.
fact: Custom modes can store separate setups for perched wildlife and fast action.
